summary.text: Writing the change in each binomial coefficient via shifted products \(P_t=\prod_{1\le u\le p^r,\,p\nmid u}(u+t p^r)\), exact quotient identities reduce the claim to strong divisibility of \(P_1-P_0\) and \(P_2-3P_1+2P_0\). Pairing \(u\) with \(p^r-u\) and using vanishing sums of inverse squares (and inverse fourth powers for the \(r=2,\ p\ge7\) refinement) yields these product congruences, while prime-power stability of the lower-level binomial coefficients gives the needed coefficient cancellation; the exceptional \((p,r)=(3,2),(5,2)\) second-difference congruences follow by finite arithmetic.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
a(n)=\binom{3n}{n}^{2}-27\binom{2n}{n}.
\]
We prove that, for every prime \(p\ge 3\) and every \(r\ge2\),
\[
a(p^r)\equiv a(p^{r-1})\pmod {p^{3r+3}}.
\]

Throughout, products and congruences are over the integers unless another ring is explicitly mentioned.

## 1. Unit sums modulo a prime power

We first record the power-sum facts that will control the first and second terms in our product expansions.

Let \(q=p^s\), where \(s\ge1\), and let \((\mathbb Z/q\mathbb Z)^\times\) be the group of units modulo \(q\).

### Reciprocal squares for \(p\ge5\)

If \(p\ge5\), then
\[
\sum_{x\in(\mathbb Z/q\mathbb Z)^\times}x^2=0\quad\text{in }\mathbb Z/q\mathbb Z.
\]
Indeed, multiplication by \(2\) permutes the unit group. Thus, writing the sum as \(S\),
\[
S=\sum_x(2x)^2=4S,
\]
so \(3S=0\). Since \(p\ge5\), the integer \(3\) is invertible modulo \(q\), and hence \(S=0\).

Inversion also permutes the unit group, so
\[
\sum_{x\in(\mathbb Z/q\mathbb Z)^\times}x^{-2}=0\pmod q. \tag{1}
\]

Because \(q\) is odd, the nonzero residue classes prime to \(p\) split into pairs \(\{u,q-u\}\), with one member satisfying \(1\le u<q/2\). Since
\[
(q-u)^{-2}=(-u)^{-2}=u^{-2}\pmod q,
\]
(1) is twice the corresponding half-sum. The factor \(2\) is invertible modulo \(q\), so
\[
\sum_{\substack{1\le u<q/2\\p\nmid u}}u^{-2}\equiv0\pmod q. \tag{2}
\]

### Reciprocal squares for \(p=3\)

For \(q=3^s\), the same multiplication-by-\(2\) argument gives
\[
S=4S,
\]
and therefore only
\[
3S=0\pmod q.
\]
After inversion and pairing \(u\) with \(q-u\), we obtain
\[
3\sum_{\substack{1\le u<q/2\\3\nmid u}}u^{-2}\equiv0\pmod q. \tag{3}
\]
Equivalently, if integer representatives are chosen for the inverses, the half-sum is divisible by \(3^{s-1}\).

### Reciprocal fourth powers for \(p\ge7\)

If \(p\ge7\), multiplication by \(2\) gives, for
\(T=\sum x^4\),
\[
T=16T,
\]
so \(15T=0\pmod q\). Since neither \(3\) nor \(5\) equals \(p\), the integer \(15\) is invertible modulo \(q\). Consequently
\[
\sum_{x\in(\mathbb Z/q\mathbb Z)^\times}x^{-4}=0\pmod q.
\]
Pairing again, and cancelling \(2\), yields
\[
\sum_{\substack{1\le u<q/2\\p\nmid u}}u^{-4}\equiv0\pmod q. \tag{4}
\]

## 2. Unit products and pairing

Fix an odd prime \(p\), let \(q=p^s\), and define
\[
P_t(q):=\prod_{\substack{1\le u\le q\\p\nmid u}}(u+tq)
       =\prod_{\substack{1\le u<q\\p\nmid u}}(u+tq)
\qquad(t\ge0).
\]
(The possible endpoint \(u=q\) is omitted automatically because it is divisible by \(p\).)

Pairing the factor indexed by \(u\), where \(1\le u<q/2\), with the factor indexed by \(q-u\), gives
\[
(u+tq)(q-u+tq)
 =u(q-u)+t(t+1)q^2.
\]
Thus, if
\[
H=\{u:1\le u<q/2,\ p\nmid u\},
\qquad A_u=u(q-u),
\]
then
\[
P_t(q)=\prod_{u\in H}\bigl(A_u+t(t+1)q^2\bigr). \tag{5}
\]
In particular, the constants \(t(t+1)\) for \(t=0,1,2\) are respectively \(0,2,6\).

For each \(u\in H\), we have
\[
A_u=u(q-u)\equiv-u^2\pmod q.
\]
Choose an integer \(B_u\) satisfying
\[
B_u\equiv-u^{-2}\pmod q.
\]
Then
\[
A_uB_u\equiv1\pmod q. \tag{6}
\]
By (2), for \(p\ge5\),
\[
\sum_{u\in H}B_u\equiv0\pmod q. \tag{7}
\]
For \(p=3\), (3) gives the weaker assertion
\[
3^{s-1}\mid\sum_{u\in H}B_u. \tag{8}
\]
For \(p\ge7\), since \(B_u^2\equiv u^{-4}\pmod q\), (4) also gives
\[
\sum_{u\in H}B_u^2\equiv0\pmod q. \tag{9}
\]

We shall use two elementary product expansions.

### First-order product expansion

Suppose that \(A_iB_i\equiv1\pmod q\) for every member of a finite index set. Then, for every integer \(c\),
\[
\prod_i(A_i+cq^2)
\equiv
\left(\prod_iA_i\right)
\left(1+cq^2\sum_iB_i\right)
\pmod{q^3}. \tag{10}
\]

This can be proved directly by induction on the number of factors. When one more factor is inserted, all terms involving two perturbations \(cq^2\) are divisible by \(q^4\), hence by \(q^3\). In the linear term one may replace the inverse of \(A_i\) by \(B_i\), because \(A_iB_i-1\) is divisible by \(q\), and multiplication by \(q^2\) then makes the resulting error divisible by \(q^3\).

Combining (7) with (10), for \(p\ge5\) we find
\[
P_t(q)\equiv P_0(q)\pmod{q^3}.
\]
Since \(q=p^s\), this says
\[
p^{3s}\mid P_t(p^s)-P_0(p^s)\qquad(p\ge5). \tag{11}
\]

For \(p=3\), the same expansion and (8) show that its linear correction is divisible by
\[
q^2\cdot3^{s-1}=3^{3s-1},
\]
while its error is divisible by \(q^3=3^{3s}\). Therefore
\[
3^{3s-1}\mid P_t(3^s)-P_0(3^s). \tag{12}
\]

### A second-difference product identity

For any finite set and any integers \(F_i,x\), one has
\[
x^2\mid
\prod_i(F_i+6x)-3\prod_i(F_i+2x)+2\prod_iF_i. \tag{13}
\]
This follows either by expanding the products or by induction. The constant terms cancel because \(1-3+2=0\), and the terms linear in \(x\) cancel because \(6-3\cdot2=0\); every surviving term contains at least \(x^2\).

Apply (13) to \(F_i=A_u\) and \(x=q^2\). By (5),
\[
q^4\mid P_2(q)-3P_1(q)+2P_0(q). \tag{14}
\]
If \(s\ge3\), then \(4s\ge3s+3\), so (14) implies
\[
p^{3s+3}\mid P_2(p^s)-3P_1(p^s)+2P_0(p^s). \tag{15}
\]
This is valid for every odd prime \(p\).

We need a stronger version of (14) when \(s=2\) and \(p\ge7\). We state the relevant refined expansion. Suppose \(m\mid y\) and \(A_iB_i\equiv1\pmod m\). Then
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\prod_i(A_i+6y)-3\prod_i(A_i+2y)+2\prod_iA_i\\
&\quad\equiv
12\left(\prod_iA_i\right)y^2
\left(\left(\sum_iB_i\right)^2-\sum_iB_i^2\right)
\pmod{my^2}. \tag{16}
\end{aligned}
\]
To justify (16), expand the products to second order. Constant and first-order terms cancel as above. The second-order term in \(\prod(A_i+cy)\) is
\[
c^2y^2\left(\prod_iA_i\right)\sum_{i<j}B_iB_j
\]
modulo \(my^2\), because each \(B_i\) is an inverse to \(A_i\) modulo \(m\). The coefficient in the indicated second difference is
\(6^2-3\cdot2^2=24\). Since
\[
2\sum_{i<j}B_iB_j=\left(\sum_iB_i\right)^2-\sum_iB_i^2,
\]
this gives the coefficient \(12\) in (16). Every term of degree at least three contains \(y^3\), which is divisible by \(my^2\) because \(m\mid y\). This proves (16).

Now let \(q=p^2\), \(p\ge7\), and put \(y=q^2=p^4\). From (7) and (9), both \(\sum B_u\) and \(\sum B_u^2\) are divisible by \(q\), and in particular by \(p\). Hence
\[
p\mid \left(\sum B_u\right)^2-\sum B_u^2.
\]
Taking \(m=p\) in (16), its correction term is divisible by \(py^2=p^9\), as is its error. Consequently
\[
p^9\mid P_2(p^2)-3P_1(p^2)+2P_0(p^2)
\qquad(p\ge7). \tag{17}
\]

The two remaining second-difference boundary cases are direct finite product evaluations.

For \((p,q)=(3,9)\), the allowed values of \(u\) are
\(1,2,4,5,7,8\), and
\[
P_0=2240,\qquad P_1=5\,445\,440,\qquad P_2=124\,982\,000.
\]
Therefore
\[
P_2-3P_1+2P_0=108\,650\,160=3^{10}\cdot1840,
\]
which is in particular divisible by \(3^9\). Thus
\[
3^9\mid P_2(9)-3P_1(9)+2P_0(9). \tag{18}
\]

For \((p,q)=(5,25)\), the allowed values are
\[
1,2,3,4,6,7,8,9,11,12,13,14,16,17,18,19,21,22,23,24.
\]
The products are
\[
\begin{aligned}
P_0&=41\,363\,226\,782\,215\,962\,624,\\
P_1&=20\,749\,010\,245\,088\,036\,145\,007\,111\,962\,624,\\
P_2&=724\,352\,980\,867\,997\,539\,725\,710\,608\,903\,962\,624.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus
\[
\begin{aligned}
P_2-3P_1+2P_0
&=724\,290\,733\,837\,262\,358\,343\,729\,152\,000\,000\,000\\
&=5^9\cdot370\,836\,855\,724\,678\,327\,471\,989\,325\,824.
\end{aligned}
\]
Hence
\[
5^9\mid P_2(25)-3P_1(25)+2P_0(25). \tag{19}
\]

## 3. Removing the multiples of \(p\) from a binomial coefficient

We next derive the exact identity linking the unit products to binomial coefficients.

For integers \(m\ge1\) and \(q\ge1\),
\[
\binom{mq}{q}\,q!=\prod_{u=1}^{q}((m-1)q+u). \tag{20}
\]
Now suppose \(q=pq_0\). Split both products in (20) into factors indexed by multiples of \(p\) and factors indexed by integers prime to \(p\). The multiple-of-\(p\) part of \(q!\) is
\[
\prod_{j=1}^{q_0}pj=p^{q_0}q_0!,
\]
and the multiple-of-\(p\) part on the right side is
\[
\prod_{j=1}^{q_0}\bigl((m-1)pq_0+pj\bigr)
=p^{q_0}\prod_{j=1}^{q_0}((m-1)q_0+j).
\]
Using (20) once more at level \(q_0\), and cancelling the common positive factors, gives the exact identity
\[
\binom{mq}{q}P_0(q)=\binom{mq_0}{q_0}P_{m-1}(q). \tag{21}
\]

In particular, with \(q=p^s\), \(q_0=p^{s-1}\), define
\[
B=\binom{3q}{q},\quad B_0=\binom{3q_0}{q_0},
\qquad
D=\binom{2q}{q},\quad D_0=\binom{2q_0}{q_0}.
\]
Then (21) gives
\[
BP_0=B_0P_2,
\qquad
DP_0=D_0P_1. \tag{22}
\]

## 4. The coefficient cancellations

We shall need congruences for the lower-level coefficients \(B_0,D_0\).

### The case \(p\ge5\)

For every \(m\ge1\) and \(s\ge1\), (21) and (11), with \(t=m-1\), imply
\[
\binom{mp^s}{p^s}P_0(p^s)
\equiv
\binom{mp^{s-1}}{p^{s-1}}P_0(p^s)
\pmod{p^3}.
\]
Every factor of \(P_0(p^s)\) is prime to \(p\), so the product is invertible modulo \(p^3\). Cancelling it gives
\[
\binom{mp^s}{p^s}\equiv
\binom{mp^{s-1}}{p^{s-1}}
\pmod{p^3}.
\]
Iterating down to \(s=0\), where \(\binom m1=m\), yields
\[
\binom{mp^s}{p^s}\equiv m\pmod{p^3}. \tag{23}
\]
Taking \(m=3\) and \(m=2\), we obtain
\[
\binom{3p^s}{p^s}\equiv3,
\qquad
\binom{2p^s}{p^s}\equiv2
\pmod{p^3}.
\]
It follows immediately that
\[
p^3\mid
2\binom{3p^s}{p^s}^{2}-9\binom{2p^s}{p^s}. \tag{24}
\]
Indeed the expression is congruent to \(2\cdot3^2-9\cdot2=0\).

### The case \(p=3\)

For \(s\ge2\), identity (21) and (12) imply stability modulo \(3^4=81\), because
\(3s-1\ge4\):
\[
\binom{m3^s}{3^s}\equiv
\binom{m3^{s-1}}{3^{s-1}}
\pmod{81}.
\]
Iterating down to \(s=1\), we get
\[
\binom{m3^s}{3^s}\equiv\binom{3m}{3}\pmod{81}
\qquad(s\ge1). \tag{25}
\]
For \(m=3\) and \(m=2\), the base values are
\[
\binom93=84,
\qquad
\binom63=20.
\]
Since
\[
2\cdot84^2-9\cdot20=13\,932=81\cdot172,
\]
(25) gives
\[
3^4\mid
2\binom{3\cdot3^s}{3^s}^{2}-9\binom{2\cdot3^s}{3^s}
\qquad(s\ge1). \tag{26}
\]

## 5. Algebraic assembly of the congruence

Fix now \(r\ge2\), put \(q=p^r\), \(q_0=p^{r-1}\), and abbreviate
\[
B_0=\binom{3q_0}{q_0},
\qquad D_0=\binom{2q_0}{q_0},
\qquad P_j=P_j(q)\quad(j=0,1,2).
\]
Also set
\[
\Delta_1=P_1-P_0,
\qquad
\Delta_2=P_2-3P_1+2P_0.
\]
Then
\[
P_2-P_0=3\Delta_1+\Delta_2. \tag{27}
\]
A direct algebraic rearrangement gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
&B_0^2(P_2^2-P_0^2)-27D_0P_0(P_1-P_0)\\
&\quad=\Delta_1\bigl(3B_0^2(P_2+P_0)-27D_0P_0\bigr)
 +\Delta_2B_0^2(P_2+P_0). \tag{28}
\end{aligned}
\]
The coefficient of \(\Delta_1\) can itself be rewritten as
\[
\begin{aligned}
3B_0^2(P_2+P_0)-27D_0P_0
&=3P_0(2B_0^2-9D_0)+3B_0^2(P_2-P_0). \tag{29}
\end{aligned}
\]

Suppose first that \(p\ge5\). By (11),
\[
p^{3r}\mid\Delta_1,
\qquad p^3\mid P_2-P_0. \tag{30}
\]
By (24), applied with \(s=r-1\),
\[
p^3\mid2B_0^2-9D_0. \tag{31}
\]
Equations (29)–(31) show that the coefficient of \(\Delta_1\) in (28) is divisible by \(p^3\). Thus its contribution is divisible by \(p^{3r+3}\). If, in addition,
\[
p^{3r+3}\mid\Delta_2, \tag{32}
\]
then the second term in (28) is also divisible by \(p^{3r+3}\). Hence
\[
p^{3r+3}\mid
B_0^2(P_2^2-P_0^2)-27D_0P_0(P_1-P_0). \tag{33}
\]

For \(p=3\), (12) gives
\[
3^{3r-1}\mid\Delta_1,
\qquad3^{3r-1}\mid P_2-P_0. \tag{34}
\]
By (26),
\[
3^4\mid2B_0^2-9D_0. \tag{35}
\]
Because \(r\ge2\), we have \(3r-1\ge4\). Thus (29), (34), and (35) show that the coefficient of \(\Delta_1\) is divisible by \(3^4\). Its product with \(\Delta_1\) is therefore divisible by
\[
3^{(3r-1)+4}=3^{3r+3}.
\]
If
\[
3^{3r+3}\mid\Delta_2, \tag{36}
\]
then (28) again implies (33), with \(p=3\).

It remains to connect (33) to the desired expression. Let
\[
B=\binom{3q}{q},\qquad D=\binom{2q}{q}.
\]
From (22), \(BP_0=B_0P_2\) and \(DP_0=D_0P_1\). Therefore
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\bigl((B^2-27D)-(B_0^2-27D_0)\bigr)P_0^2\\
&\quad=B_0^2(P_2^2-P_0^2)-27D_0P_0(P_1-P_0). \tag{37}
\end{aligned}
\]
Every factor in \(P_0\) is prime to \(p\), so \(P_0^2\) is invertible modulo every power of \(p\). Thus (33) and (37) allow us to cancel \(P_0^2\), obtaining
\[
B^2-27D\equiv B_0^2-27D_0\pmod{p^{3r+3}}.
\]
This is exactly
\[
a(p^r)\equiv a(p^{r-1})\pmod{p^{3r+3}}. \tag{38}
\]

## 6. Verification of the required second-difference divisibility

We finally check (32) or (36) in all cases.

* If \(r\ge3\), (15) gives
  \[
  p^{3r+3}\mid P_2(p^r)-3P_1(p^r)+2P_0(p^r)
  \]
  for every odd prime \(p\). Thus the preceding assembly proves (38) both for \(p=3\) and for \(p\ge5\).

* If \(r=2\) and \(p\ge7\), (17) gives precisely
  \[
  p^9\mid P_2(p^2)-3P_1(p^2)+2P_0(p^2),
  \]
  and \(9=3r+3\). Hence (32) holds.

* If \((p,r)=(5,2)\), the explicit evaluation (19) supplies (32), again with modulus \(5^9\).

* If \((p,r)=(3,2)\), the explicit evaluation (18) supplies (36), with modulus \(3^9\).

These cases exhaust all primes \(p\ge3\) and all integers \(r\ge2\). Therefore, for every such \(p,r\),
\[
\boxed{\displaystyle a(p^r)\equiv a(p^{r-1})\pmod{p^{3r+3}}}.
\]
